title: Herodias is one of the most haunting women in all of Scripture.
paragraphs: Herodias is one of the most haunting women in all of Scripture.
Not because Scripture spends many chapters on her.
It does not.
But because in only a few verses, God exposes something terrifying about the human heart when lust, pride, bitterness, political ambition, and hatred toward truth are left unrepented.
Her story is not ultimately about seduction.
It is about rebellion against God’s order.
It is about a woman who hated the voice that confronted her sin.
And in the end… that hatred demanded a prophet’s head.
The tragedy of Herodias is not merely historical.
It is spiritual.

Because there are still people today who do not mind hearing preaching…
until the preaching touches the thing they refuse to surrender.
And that is where Herodias becomes terrifyingly relevant.
The primary accounts concerning Herodias are found in Gospel of Matthew 14:1–12 and Gospel of Mark 6:14–29.
To understand her properly, we must first understand the corrupted family she belonged to.
Herodias was the granddaughter of Herod the Great.
The same Herod who attempted to murder the infant Christ in Bethlehem.
Already, the spiritual atmosphere surrounding this dynasty was dark, paranoid, violent, and consumed with power.
Herodias first married Herod Philip, who was her half-uncle.
Later, she abandoned him and entered into a relationship with another uncle — Herod Antipas.
This was not simply scandalous culturally.
It was unlawful before God.
John the Baptist publicly confronted this union.
And that confrontation ignited the rage that would eventually lead to his death.
The Greek text in Mark 6:18 says:
“Οὐκ ἔξεστίν σοι ἔχειν τὴν γυναῖκα τοῦ ἀδελφοῦ σου.”
Transliterated:
“Ouk exestin soi echein tēn gunaika tou adelphou sou.”
Literal translation:
“It is not lawful for you to have your brother’s wife.”
The phrase “οὐκ ἔξεστίν” (ouk exestin) means “it is not permitted” or “it is unlawful.”
John was not giving personal opinion.
He was declaring divine law.
This statement reaches back into the Torah itself.
In the Hebrew Scriptures, Leviticus 18:16 says:
“עֶרְוַת אֵשֶׁת אָחִיךָ לֹא תְגַלֵּה”
Transliteration:
“Ervat eshet achikha lo tegalleh.”
Literal meaning:
“You shall not uncover the nakedness of your brother’s wife.”
And again in Leviticus 20:21:
“וְאִישׁ אֲשֶׁר יִקַּח אֶת־אֵשֶׁת אָחִיו”
“Ve’ish asher yiqqach et-eshet achiv…”
“If a man takes his brother’s wife…”
The law declared such a union disgraceful outside the specific levirate marriage exception described elsewhere in Torah.
John the Baptist was not being politically rebellious.
He was being faithful.
That is important.
Because modern culture often reframes biblical confrontation as hatred.
But biblical truth spoken in righteousness is love.
John loved God enough to speak truth.
And he loved sinners enough to warn them.
Herod Antipas feared John.
But Herodias hated him.
Mark 6:19 says:
“Ἡ δὲ Ἡρῳδιὰς ἐνεῖχεν αὐτῷ”
“Hē de Hērōdias eneichen autō.”
This Greek phrase is powerful.
The verb “ἐνεῖχεν” (eneichen) carries the idea of holding a grudge, bearing hostility, nursing resentment.
Herodias did not merely dislike John.
She harbored deep, simmering hatred against the man exposing her sin.
And this is one of the clearest revelations of unrepentant human nature in Scripture:
People often do not hate darkness until someone turns on the light.
John’s holiness exposed Herodias.
His courage stripped away her self-justification.
His voice became unbearable because conviction was piercing her conscience.
This is why many people avoid truth-filled preaching.
Not because they cannot understand it.
But because truth threatens the kingdom they built around their sin.
Herodias represents the soul that would rather silence conviction than repent.
And eventually, opportunity arrived.
Mark 6 describes Herod’s birthday feast.
A royal environment filled with intoxication, ego, lust, political performance, and reckless vows.
Herodias’ daughter danced before the guests.
Tradition later identifies her as Salome, though Scripture itself does not directly name her in these passages.
Herod, intoxicated by pride and desire, made a foolish oath.
Mark 6:23:
“Whatever you ask me, I will give you, up to half my kingdom.”
This echoes the language of pagan kings in the ancient world.
It is theatrical power-talk.
Emotion ruling wisdom.
Pride ruling discernment.
And Herodias immediately saw her moment.
Mark 6:24–25 records the daughter consulting her mother.
The Greek says:
“Τί αἰτήσωμαι;”
“What shall I ask?”
Herodias answered:
“Τὴν κεφαλὴν Ἰωάννου τοῦ βαπτίζοντος.”
“The head of John the Baptist.”
Not imprisonment.
Not exile.
Not silence.
His head.
This is what hatred does when sin hardens the heart long enough.
Conviction becomes so intolerable that the conscience seeks to destroy the messenger.
And the daughter returned “μετὰ σπουδῆς” — “with haste” or “immediately.”
The request becomes even more horrifying in Greek:
“θέλω ἵνα ἐξαυτῆς δῷς μοι”
“I want you to give me at once…”
The urgency reveals something dark.
Hatred had been waiting for this opportunity.
Herod was grieved.
Mark says:
“περίλυπος γενόμενος”
“Having become deeply distressed.”
Yet he still obeyed the wicked request.
Why?
Because fear of man ruled him more than fear of God.
This is another devastating lesson from the story.
Herod feared public embarrassment more than divine judgment.
And countless souls still destroy themselves this same way.

They know something is evil.
They know something is sinful.
They know conviction is real.
But they fear losing approval.
So they crucify conscience to protect reputation.
John the Baptist was executed in prison.

The prophet who prepared the way for Messiah…
murdered to protect the pride of adulterous rulers.
And somewhere in that palace, Herodias finally got the silence she wanted.
But only temporarily.
Because no one truly silences the truth of God.
The voice of John still speaks through Scripture thousands of years later.

And Herodias is remembered not as victorious…
but as a warning.
There is another layer many overlook.
Herodias mirrors the spirit of Jezebel in the Old Testament.
Both manipulated weak rulers.
Both opposed righteous prophets.
Both used influence to attack truth.
Both weaponized immoral environments.
Both reveal how seduction and power can become instruments of spiritual destruction.
This does not mean women are uniquely dangerous.
Scripture equally condemns wicked men.
Herod himself was guilty.
But Herodias demonstrates how influence without repentance becomes corruption.
Power without submission to God becomes destructive.
And beauty without holiness becomes dangerous to both self and others.
Yet even in this dark story, the Gospel shines brighter.
Because Jesus Christ came for sinners exactly like Herodias.
Had she repented, grace was available.

The blood of Christ is greater than adultery.
Greater than manipulation.
Greater than hatred.
Greater than murder.
That is the scandalous beauty of the Gospel.
Even those who opposed righteousness can be redeemed through repentance and faith in Jesus Christ.
But Herodias stands as a warning of what happens when conviction is repeatedly resisted.
The human heart does not remain neutral toward truth.

It softens…
or it hardens.
Hebrews 3:15 echoes this danger:
“Today, if you hear His voice, do not harden your hearts.”
That warning still matters.
Because many people are living modern versions of Herod’s palace.

Endless entertainment.
Sexual confusion.
Public performance.
Moral compromise.
Drunken distraction.
Pride disguised as freedom.

And then a sermon appears.
A Scripture cuts deep.
A conviction rises late at night when the room becomes quiet.
That moment matters more than people realize.
Because the soul must choose:

Repent…
or silence the voice confronting the sin.
Herodias chose silence.
John lost his earthly life.
But Herodias lost something far worse.
A heart unwilling to bow before God.
And history remembers which one truly belonged to the Kingdom of Heaven.
The tragedy is not that John died.
The tragedy is that Herodias heard truth and still refused repentance.
And that danger still exists now.
That numbness is dangerous.
Very dangerous.
But Jesus Christ still calls sinners to come into the light.
Not to shame them.
To save them.
The cross proves that mercy remains available even to the guilty.
The empty tomb proves sin does not have final authority over those who repent and believe.
And the same God who exposed Herodias still offers forgiveness today through Christ alone.
Not self-improvement.
Not religion.
Not image management.

Repentance.
Faith.
Surrender to Jesus Christ.
That is the only path that leads from death into life.
